paragraphs.title: Introduction and the Parable of Assyria

answers: Pharaoh king of Egypt and his multitude
The king of Assyria only
The trees of the field
easy.explanation: The Lord told Ezekiel to speak unto Pharaoh king of Egypt and to his multitude.
easy.q: To whom was Ezekiel told to speak?

answers: A cedar in Lebanon
A great river
A high mountain
easy.explanation: The Assyrian was described as a cedar in Lebanon.
easy.q: What was the Assyrian compared to?

answers: The eleventh year
The third year
The first year
easy.explanation: The prophecy came in the eleventh year, in the third month, on the first day of the month.
easy.q: In which year did this prophecy come to Ezekiel?

answers: To provide a comparison for Egypt’s greatness
To describe Israel’s journey
To explain the source of Lebanon’s waters
medium.explanation: Assyria’s greatness served as the example by which Pharaoh could measure his own greatness.
medium.q: Why was Assyria presented before Pharaoh?

answers: Who could be compared with him in greatness
Where he would go after death
Who gave him water
medium.explanation: The question challenges Pharaoh to consider what ruler or kingdom could be compared with his greatness.
medium.q: What does the question “Whom art thou like in thy greatness?” ask Pharaoh to consider?

answers: Assyria is used as an example of great power against which Pharaoh is measured
Assyria is shown as a nation Pharaoh must protect
Assyria is identified as Ezekiel’s dwelling place
medium.explanation: The mighty cedar represents Assyria and prepares the comparison with Egypt.
medium.q: What connection is made between Pharaoh and the description of Assyria?

answers: It makes Pharaoh examine the extent of his own greatness
It announces that Pharaoh has already descended into the grave
It gives the number of trees in Lebanon
challenge.explanation: The question turns Pharaoh’s attention to the measure and limits of his greatness.
challenge.q: What is the literary purpose of the opening question to Pharaoh?

answers: It was a high cedar with its top among the thick boughs
It was a small tree in an open field
It was planted in the nether parts of the earth
challenge.explanation: Its height and position among the thick boughs emphasize its strength and majesty.
challenge.q: Which detail in verse 3 strengthens the picture of Assyria’s power?

answers: They give the date, address Pharaoh, and introduce Assyria as a cedar
They give only the place and describe Egypt as a river
They address Assyria and describe only the trees of Eden
challenge.explanation: The passage first gives the date, then names Pharaoh, and then introduces the cedar image.
challenge.q: How do the opening verses combine time, audience, and symbol?

paragraphs.title: The Cedar’s Growth and Assyria’s Protection

answers: The waters and the deep
A strong wind
The cutting down of other trees
easy.explanation: The waters made the cedar great and the deep set it up on high.
easy.q: What caused the cedar to grow great?

answers: Many great nations
Only the trees of Eden
Only the fowls of heaven
easy.explanation: The passage says that under its shadow dwelt all great nations.
easy.q: Who dwelt under the cedar’s shadow?

answers: As unmatched in beauty
As the lowest of all the trees
As dry and without branches
easy.explanation: No tree in the garden of God was like it in beauty.
easy.q: How was the cedar described among the other trees?

answers: The resources and power that strengthened Assyria
The enemies that destroyed Assyria
The grave to which Assyria descended
medium.explanation: The waters symbolize the resources and support that enabled Assyria to grow powerful.
medium.q: What do the abundant waters represent in the picture of Assyria?

answers: Large branches
Roots beneath the ground
Enemies of the tree
medium.explanation: Boughs are the large branches of a tree.

answers: Its size and strength provided shelter
It had fallen into the ground
There was no water in the land
medium.explanation: The mighty cedar offered protection and shelter to many nations.
medium.q: Why did many nations dwell under the cedar’s shadow?

answers: Its growth represents Assyria’s strengthening and expanding influence
Its cutting down represents Assyria’s increase
Its drying up represents Assyria’s greater power
challenge.explanation: The cedar’s growth and spreading branches picture the expansion of Assyria’s influence.
challenge.q: How does the cedar’s spreading growth portray Assyria’s power?

answers: Its influence and protection reached many kinds of creatures and peoples
It stood alone in a lifeless wilderness
It served only as a nesting place for birds
challenge.explanation: The many creatures and nations show the wide reach of the cedar’s shelter and influence.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the presence of birds, beasts, and nations around the cedar?

answers: The cedar’s unique beauty and superiority
The cedar’s weakness compared with every other tree
The cedar’s ordinary and unremarkable nature
challenge.explanation: The other trees were not like its branches, showing that it was unmatched.
challenge.q: What does the comparison with cedars, fir trees, and chestnut trees emphasize?

answers: It lifted itself up in pride
It lacked water
It refused to shelter the nations
easy.explanation: The cedar became proud because it was exalted in height.

answers: The mighty one of the heathen
The trees of Eden
The fowls of heaven
easy.explanation: God delivered the cedar into the hand of the mighty one of the heathen.
easy.q: Into whose hand was the cedar delivered?

answers: They went down from its shadow and left it
They made it grow larger
They hid within its top
easy.explanation: After its fall, all the people went down from its shadow and abandoned it.
easy.q: What happened to the people who had lived under the cedar’s shadow?

answers: Its pride led to God delivering it into the hand of a mighty nation
Its pride caused the waters to make it greater
Its pride caused the nations to remain loyal to it
medium.explanation: Because it lifted itself up, God gave it over to judgment.
medium.q: What was the connection between Assyria’s pride and its fall?

answers: The spreading limbs of the tree
The waters surrounding the tree
The nations that served it
medium.explanation: The word refers to the limbs or boughs extending from the cedar.
medium.q: In the KJV, what are “branches” in this context?

answers: Assyria’s power was broken and dispersed
Assyria continued ruling all the nations
The cedar became more beautiful after being cut down
medium.explanation: The broken and fallen branches picture the collapse of Assyria’s power.
medium.q: What does the cutting off and scattering of the cedar’s branches show?

answers: A power that exalts itself will eventually descend to death
Every great tree will always be protected
Nations do not need leaders
challenge.explanation: The fall warns that pride and greatness cannot prevent judgment and death.
challenge.q: What general lesson comes from Assyria’s fall?

answers: They sheltered under it before the fall but abandoned it afterward
They cut it down before the fall and grew it afterward
They ignored it before the fall but worshiped it afterward
challenge.explanation: The nations first depended on the cedar, but they left it once its power was broken.
challenge.q: How did the nations’ relationship to the cedar change before and after its fall?

answers: They were not to exalt themselves because of their height and strength
They were to learn how to grow beside streams
They were to compete with the cedar in beauty
challenge.explanation: The fall warned all proud powers that they too were subject to death.
challenge.q: Why was the cedar’s fall a warning to the other trees by the waters?

paragraphs.title: Descent to Sheol and the Message to Pharaoh

answers: It mourned and became darkened in sorrow
It was filled with light
It became a desert
easy.explanation: The Lord caused Lebanon to mourn, and the trees of the field fainted.
easy.q: What happened to Lebanon when the cedar went down to the grave?

answers: To the nether parts of the earth
To the top of Lebanon
To the garden of God
easy.explanation: The cedar and, by application, Pharaoh descend to the nether parts of the earth.
easy.q: Where did the cedar and Pharaoh descend?

answers: The trees of Eden
The fowls of heaven
The kings of Egypt
easy.explanation: The trees of Eden were comforted when the mighty cedar joined them in death.
easy.q: Who was comforted in the nether parts of the earth?

answers: They were shaken by the sound of its fall
They rebuilt the cedar
They continued dwelling safely under its shadow
medium.explanation: The nations were made to shake when God cast the cedar down.
medium.q: How did the cedar’s fall affect the nations?

answers: The dead who descend to the place of death
People going down to draw water
Servants descending from a mountain
medium.explanation: The phrase refers to those who descend into the grave or realm of the dead.
medium.q: What does the phrase “them that descend into the pit” mean in this passage?

answers: Pharaoh and his multitude will also descend to the nether parts of the earth
Pharaoh will sit under the cedar’s shadow
Pharaoh will restore Assyria’s greatness
medium.explanation: The final verse directly applies the cedar’s fate to Pharaoh and all his multitude.
medium.q: How is Assyria’s fate applied to Pharaoh?

answers: It frightens the living but shows the fallen that even the greatest power descends to death
It makes the nations rejoice and brings the cedar back to life
It causes the trees to grow and the nations to hide
challenge.explanation: The fall is terrifying to the nations, yet comforting to the dead because another mighty ruler has joined them.
challenge.q: Why does the cedar’s fall both shake the nations and comfort the trees of Eden?

answers: The mourning expresses the grief and loss caused by the cedar’s downfall
The mourning celebrates the cedar’s renewed strength
The mourning means that all the waters stopped flowing
challenge.explanation: Lebanon’s mourning symbolizes the sorrow and dramatic change brought by the cedar’s fall.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between Lebanon’s mourning and the cedar’s descent?

answers: Even Pharaoh, despite his glory and greatness, will share the fate of proud powers
Pharaoh is greater than Assyria and cannot be judged
Pharaoh will receive the trees of Eden and rule forever
challenge.explanation: The fate of Assyria is presented as a warning that Pharaoh and his multitude will also be brought down.
challenge.q: What is the final message of the chapter concerning Pharaoh?
